questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) Distinguish between weather and climate.

(3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Weather** is the state of the atmosphere (temperature, rainfall, humidity, pressure, wind, cloud and sunshine) of a place over a **short time**: an hour, a day or a week. It changes quickly and often (for example "it rained heavily in Douala this afternoon").

**Climate** is the **average** weather conditions of a place measured over a **long period**, usually at least **30 years**, and includes the usual range and seasons (for example "the Cameroon coast has a hot, wet climate with a long rainy season").

| | Weather | Climate |
|---|---|---|
| Time | short term (hours, days) | long term (30 years or more) |
| Nature | the actual, changing condition | the average and the pattern |
| Variability | changes quickly | changes very slowly |
| Study | observed daily by weather stations | worked out from long records (averages) |

**Conclusion:** weather is what you get on a given day; climate is what you expect over the years.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) (i) Name **ONE** erosional and **ONE** depositional feature from each of the following areas:

**Coast land, river valley and hot desert.**

(4 marks)

(ii) Draw **ONE** erosional and **ONE** depositional feature, from the features named.

(4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Features named (4 marks).**

| Area | Erosional feature | Depositional feature |
|---|---|---|
| **Coast land** | cliff (also wave-cut platform, cave, arch, stack) | beach (also spit, bar, tombolo) |
| **River valley** | waterfall (also V-shaped valley, gorge) | flood plain (also levee, delta, meander deposits) |
| **Hot desert** | mushroom rock (rock pedestal) (also wadi, inselberg) | sand dune, e.g. a barchan (also alluvial fan) |

**(ii) Drawings (4 marks).** Draw each feature large, in pencil, with a title and labels. Two models:

**1. A waterfall (erosional feature, river valley).** Draw a side view of a river flowing from left to right over a step. Label: the **hard (resistant) rock** forming the cap at the top; the **soft (less resistant) rock** underneath, worn away faster by the water and by the swirling stones; the **overhang** (the hard rock left sticking out); the **plunge pool** at the foot, deepened by the force of the falling water; the **gorge** downstream, formed as the fall retreats upstream; the direction of flow. Title: "A waterfall".

**2. A spit (depositional feature, coast).** Draw a plan view of a coastline that bends sharply. Label: the **mainland**; the **spit**, a long narrow ridge of sand and shingle joined to the land at one end and ending in the sea; the **hooked (curved) end**; the **direction of longshore drift** along the coast; the **prevailing wind and waves**; the **sheltered water** with a salt marsh behind the spit. Title: "A spit".

(Any other correct, well-labelled drawing of a feature named in (i), for example a cliff and wave-cut platform or a sand dune, earns the marks. The marks are for the drawing, the labels and the title.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) Outline the pressure and wind belts of the globe using a well annotated diagram.

(4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The pressure belts of the globe are caused by unequal heating (the equator is heated most) and by the rotation of the earth. Winds blow on the surface from the **high-pressure belts** to the **low-pressure belts**, and the rotation of the earth (the Coriolis effect) turns them to the right in the northern hemisphere and to the left in the southern hemisphere.

![fig-1](gce-ol-geography-2021-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_2_fig_1.png)

**The pressure belts (from the equator to the poles, in each hemisphere):**

1. **Equatorial low pressure (about 0 degrees), the doldrums**: hot air rises, so the pressure is low and the winds are light and variable (calms), with heavy convectional rain. The trade winds meet here (the Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone, ITCZ).
2. **Sub-tropical high pressure (about 30 degrees N and S)**: air sinks, so the pressure is high; the weather is dry and calm (the "horse latitudes"), and the hot deserts lie here.
3. **Sub-polar low pressure (about 60 degrees N and S)**: warm westerly winds meet cold polar winds and rise, so the pressure is low and the weather is stormy and changeable.
4. **Polar high pressure (about 90 degrees N and S)**: very cold air sinks, so the pressure is high.

**The wind belts (surface winds):**

1. **Trade winds**, from the sub-tropical highs to the equatorial low: the **north-east trades** in the northern hemisphere and the **south-east trades** in the southern hemisphere.
2. **Westerlies**, from the sub-tropical highs to the sub-polar lows: **south-westerlies** in the north and **north-westerlies** in the south.
3. **Polar easterlies**, from the polar highs to the sub-polar lows: **from the north-east** in the north and **from the south-east** in the south.

*Marks:* a clear diagram with the latitudes (1); the four pressure belts named (1); the three wind belts named with their direction (1); arrows and labels correct (1).

questions.enonce_markdown:
(d) Name **TWO** human causes of global warming.

(2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
1. **Burning of fossil fuels** (coal, oil and gas) in factories, power stations, vehicles and homes, which releases large amounts of **carbon dioxide** into the atmosphere.
2. **Deforestation** (clearing and burning of forests for farming, timber, charcoal and building), which releases carbon dioxide and reduces the number of trees that absorb it.

(Other accepted answers: the use of CFCs in refrigerators and aerosols; the release of methane from cattle rearing, rice fields and rubbish dumps; the use of fertilisers that release nitrous oxide.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
(e) What **THREE** ways can be used by man to stay safely in areas affected by earthquake hazards?

(3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
1. **Build earthquake-resistant buildings:** strong, light and flexible structures (steel or reinforced frames, deep and firm foundations, low and simple buildings, light roofs), and avoid heavy brick or stone walls without reinforcement, so that houses do not collapse.
2. **Land-use planning and monitoring:** avoid building on faults, steep slopes, loose or filled ground; keep open spaces; monitor earth movements and have early-warning systems where possible.
3. **Education, preparation and emergency plans:** teach people what to do (drop, cover and hold on under a strong table; keep away from windows and falling objects; go into the open once the shaking stops), hold regular drills, keep emergency kits (water, food, first aid, torch) and organise rescue and relief services.

(Other accepted answers: fix tall furniture and tanks to the walls, switch off electricity and gas, and insure buildings.)
